turns.reply:
Below is how each layer maps to its part of the machine, why the weak ones don't work, and proposals for those plus the cabinet. I took phone screenshots of RAM, CPU, wires and the cabinet to check. I haven't written any code yet: there are questions at the end for you to answer first.

## The layers today

| Layer | What it stands for | Core mechanic | Does the mechanic match the part? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Arcade hall** (top) | the arcade as a place | walk around like in Pokémon, talk to people, collect coins | yes: coins are what you need to play |
| **Cabinet** | the machine itself | tap the coin door | there's no game here, just one tap |
| **Maze** | the game | Pac-Man, running on the emulated Z80 machine | yes |
| Board lobby | the circuit board inside the machine | walk around, talk to parts, wake them up | yes |
| -1 Screen | the picture tube | the beam lights spots on the screen as it sweeps; fix the 4 picture adjustments to get one clean picture | yes, each fix visibly repairs the picture |
| -2 Video board | the chips that make the picture | carry pixels from a tile through the palette to the DAC (the chip that turns colour numbers into the video signal) before the frame timer runs out | yes |
| -3 Work RAM | the game's memory | dodge the CPU's write head, find 4 named bytes (score, lives, positions) | no: it's a scavenger hunt |
| -4 Bus | how chips talk to each other | chip rooms behind doors that open when the chip is addressed | half |
| -5 CPU | running the program | walk the source code, jump pads on CALL/JP lines, dodge the program counter | no: you just reach routines and nothing happens |
| -6 Logic | the ghosts' chase rules | stay out of the ghosts' lines of sight, stand on their target tiles | half |
| -7 Input wires | the joystick switches | stand on switch pads to steer the real Pac-Man into the 4 corners | right idea, plays badly |

## Why the screen and video board now work

- **A few big structures:** 2–3 big walk-in boxes instead of a grid of 1000 cells.
- **Each goal makes the part do its job, and you see the result:** fixing V-HOLD stops the picture rolling.
- **One clear threat, or just a timer.**
- **Text is readable at phone size.**

## Why RAM, CPU and wires don't

- **RAM:** the screen is 32×32 cells of tiny two-digit hex. The goals are "find the byte called SCORE", and finding it changes nothing. The write head is a small red box.
- **CPU:** 51 pages of source code is the whole level. The jump pads, the Z/C flag blocks and the program counter all stack up and make the screen busy. Reaching a routine has no effect.
- **Wires:** steering a Pac-Man far away by standing on pads splits your attention. You can't stand on UP and watch the picture at the same time. The push block and the spark add rules without adding meaning.

## Proposals (same recipe as the screen and video board)

**-3 Work RAM: "poke the game state".**
- Zoom in on about 8 game variables, each a big box with its name, value and 8 bit lamps: SCORE, LIVES, PAC X/Y, BLINKY X, LEVEL, DOTS LEFT, GHOST MODE.
- A small maze picture at the top shows the game.
- Stepping on a bit lamp flips that bit, like a cheat device. Goals: make 4 changes that show up in the game, e.g. 5 lives, Blinky moved, all ghosts scared.
- The CPU's write head dashes to a variable when the program writes it, and overwrites your change. So you have to time your flips between its writes and then watch them stick. That's what RAM is: the last write wins, and the game reads whatever is there.

**-5 CPU: "Game Genie" patches.**
- One routine per screen, about 12 big lines.
- The program counter is a glowing cursor that steps line by line and visibly jumps on branches. The registers are big boxes at the bottom.
- Goals: in 4 routines, carry a patch token (a replacement instruction) onto the marked line. Each patch changes the game in the maze picture: Pac-Man faster, ghosts slower, no life lost, free extra life.
- The program counter stays the threat: it hits you if it's on your line.
- This replaces the jump pads and flag blocks.

**-7 Input wires: "fix the joystick, then play".**
- The joystick base sits in the middle with its 4 switches. Big wires run up to the IN0 port pins under the maze picture.
- The wires are broken. You carry each wire end to its pin, the same carry-and-deliver as the video board.
- Every repaired direction starts working in the maze picture. Noise sparks run along the wires as the threat.
- Once all 4 are fixed, the last goal is to swipe-play the real game for a few seconds (eat N dots) with the stick you just repaired.
- The pads and the push block go.

**Cabinet (2nd layer from the top): coin minigame.**
- All of Max's cabinet art stays as it is.
- Tapping the coin door zooms into the coin mechanism behind it, which is new art in `assets/cabinet/`. Real coin mechanisms tested coins mechanically.
- You flick the coin into the slot, then tap to time it past the reject arm and the magnet that catches fake coins.
- If it passes, it hits the coin switch, which sends a signal down a wire to the machine (the same COIN bit the input wires layer shows): CREDIT 1, and you zoom into the maze.
- If it fails, the coin drops into the coin return. You don't lose it; you retry. About 5 seconds in total.

## Questions (suggested default in *italics*)

1. **Order:** one layer per push so you can playtest each? *Default: yes, in the order cabinet coin minigame → RAM → wires → CPU.*
2. **Small maze picture at the top** of RAM, CPU and wires, so every goal shows its effect in the real game? *Default: yes, the same picture the wires layer has now.*
3. **RAM:** go with "poke the game state" (flip bits in about 8 big variable boxes, the write head overwrites you)? *Default: yes. Goals: 5 lives, move Blinky, scare the ghosts, score over 10000.*
4. **CPU:** replace the jump pads and flag blocks with Game Genie patches, one routine per screen? *Default: yes, 4 patches, keep the program counter as the threat.*
5. **Wires:** reconnect the broken wires, then play with the repaired stick? *Default: yes, drop the pads and the push block, keep the noise sparks.*
6. **Coin minigame:** coin mechanism with a timed reject arm, and a failed coin drops into the coin return without being lost? *Default: yes, every coin goes through it, about 5 s, no skip.*
7. **Cabinet while the bot plays:** add something to do there too, or only the coin minigame? *Default: only the coin minigame for now.*
8. **Art:** new pieces (coin mechanism interior, RAM boxes, joystick base) start as code-drawn placeholders for Max to replace, with Max's existing cabinet files untouched? *Default: yes.*

I haven't touched the bus or logic layers; say if you want those reworked too.

Plan usage is at 7% of the 5-hour limit and 25% of the weekly one. The four reworks are mid-sized jobs, so one at a time is the cheaper route.
